items.q: Which correlation coefficient shows the strongest relationship between two variables?

why.correct: Strength is the size of r, ignoring the sign. A coefficient near -1 or +1 is strong; near 0 is weak.
options: Right: its size, 0.82, is the largest; the minus sign gives only the direction.
Its size, 0.45, is smaller than 0.82.
This is close to zero: a very weak relationship.
Its size, 0.30, is smaller than 0.82.

items.q: Across 50 towns, the more ice cream is sold in a month, the more drownings occur. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Eating ice cream causes people to drown more often
Hot weather raises both swimming and ice cream sales
Drownings make the people of a town buy more ice cream
The relationship is likely an illusory correlation

why.correct: Two variables can move together because a third variable affects both. Hot months bring more swimming (and drownings) and more ice cream.
options: A correlation does not show cause; a third variable explains this one.
Right: summer heat drives both.
That reverses the direction, and it still ignores the obvious third variable.
An illusory correlation is a relationship people believe in that the data do not show; here the data show one.

items.q: Students who eat breakfast have higher grades. A news story says, "Breakfast boosts grades." What is the best criticism?
options: The relationship is negative, so breakfast actually lowers grades
Grades are not a variable that a behavior like breakfast can be correlated with
A correlation shows no cause; family routines may affect both
The correlation proves that grades are caused by sleep, not by breakfast

why.correct: A correlational finding does not justify "boosts". Families with regular routines may provide both breakfast and support for schoolwork.
options: Higher grades with breakfast is a positive correlation, not a negative one.
Any two measured variables can be correlated.
Right: a third variable, such as a structured home life, may explain both.
A correlation proves no cause, including sleep.

items.q: As the number of hours a teen spends on homework rises, the number of hours of free time falls. Which correlation coefficient fits best?

why.correct: When one variable goes up as the other goes down, the correlation is negative.
options: A positive r means both rise together; here one falls as the other rises.
Zero means no relationship; these two clearly move together.
r is always between -1 and +1, so 1.50 is impossible.
Right: as one rises the other falls, and the link is fairly strong.

items.q: Children who play violent video games more often are rated by teachers as more aggressive. Which is an example of the directionality problem in this finding?
options: Already aggressive children may choose violent games more
Parents’ supervision may affect both game time and aggression
Teachers who rate the children may know about their games
The children were not randomly sampled from the population of children

why.correct: The directionality problem: in a correlation we cannot tell which of the two variables affects the other.
options: Right: aggression could lead to game choice, the reverse of the usual story.
That is a third variable, a separate problem from directionality.
That is a source of bias in the measure, not directionality.
That limits generalizing; it is not about which variable came first.

items.q: A nurse is sure that more babies are born on nights with a full moon. Hospital records show no relationship between moon phase and births. What explains the nurse’s belief?
options: A negative correlation between the moon and births
An illusory correlation: busy full-moon nights stand out
A third variable that causes both full moons and births
Experimenter bias in the hospital’s birth records

why.correct: An illusory correlation is a relationship people believe in that the data do not show, often because memorable cases stand out.
options: The records show no relationship at all, positive or negative.
Right: people remember the cases that fit their belief.
There is no relationship in the records for a third variable to explain.
Experimenter bias is a researcher’s expectations shaping the data; here the records are accurate and the error is in the nurse’s memory.

items.q: Which of these describe a positive correlation? Select all that apply.
options: The more hours students sleep, the higher their quiz scores
The more a person practices piano, the fewer mistakes they make
The less people exercise, the less energy they report
Shoe size and grade average are unrelated in adults

why.correct: A positive correlation means the two variables move in the same direction, both up or both down together.
options: Right: both rise together.
Practice rises as mistakes fall: negative.
Both fall together, which is also positive.
No relationship: r near zero.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship in the scatterplot?
options: A strong negative correlation
A weak positive correlation
A strong positive correlation
No correlation between hours and scores

why.correct: The points slope upward and cluster tightly around the line of best fit: strong and positive. For these invented data r = .88.
options: The points rise from left to right, so the correlation is positive.
The points sit close to the line, so the relationship is strong.
Right: scores rise with hours and the points lie close to the line (r = .88).
There is a clear upward pattern.

items.q: A teacher concludes from this plot that studying more causes higher quiz scores. What is the problem with that conclusion?
options: The correlation is negative, so studying lowers scores
The plot shows no relationship between hours and scores
A scatterplot shows the cause, but this one has too few students
The data are correlational; interest could raise both

why.correct: The students chose how much to study, so this is a correlational study. Interest, prior knowledge or free time could affect both hours and scores. An experiment that randomly assigns study time would be needed to show cause.
options: The points rise from left to right: the correlation is positive.
There is a clear, strong pattern.
A scatterplot shows a relationship, never a cause, whatever its size.
Right: a third variable, such as interest, could explain the pattern.

items.q: Using the line of best fit, about what score would you predict for a student who studied 4 hours?
options: About 70
About 55
About 88
About 4

why.correct: The line of best fit passes near 70 at 4 hours. A correlation lets you predict one variable from the other, even though it does not show cause.
options: Right: the line passes near 70 at 4 hours.
That is near the line at 1 hour.
That is near the line at 8 hours.
That is the number of hours, not a score.

items.q: Build a statement about this scatterplot that a reader would accept.

why.correct: Name the direction and strength, then say what the correlation does and does not show.

specific.frame: Hours studied and quiz scores show ___; this means that ___.
specific.model: Hours studied and quiz scores show a strong positive correlation; this means that students who studied more tended to score higher, but the data cannot show that studying caused the higher scores.

describe.label: Relationship
options: a strong positive correlation
a strong negative correlation
a weak positive correlation

why.1: The points rise to the right: positive, not negative.
why.2: The points sit close to the line: strong, not weak.

meaning.label: Meaning
options: studying more caused every student to score higher
students who studied more tended to score higher, though the data cannot show cause
students who scored higher must have studied less

why.0: A correlation shows a tendency, not a cause, and not for every student.
why.2: That is the reverse of the pattern in the plot.

items.q: Which pair of variables has the strongest relationship?
options: Hours of sleep and daytime sleepiness rating
Phone checks per hour and distraction rating
Minutes of exercise and mood rating
Hours of part-time work and homework hours

why.correct: Compare the size of r without the sign: 0.71 is the largest.
options: Its size, 0.62, is moderate and smaller than 0.71.
Right: 0.71 is the largest size in the table.
0.31 is a weak relationship.
0.18 is weak.

items.q: What does $r = -0.62$ for sleep and daytime sleepiness mean?
options: Students who sleep more tend to report more daytime sleepiness
Sleeping more causes 62% less daytime sleepiness
Students who sleep more tend to report less daytime sleepiness
Sleep and daytime sleepiness are unrelated in teenagers

why.correct: The sign gives the direction (negative: as one rises, the other tends to fall); the size, 0.62, says the relationship is moderately strong.
options: That would be a positive correlation.
r is not a percent, and a correlation does not show cause.
Right: a negative r means one tends to fall as the other rises.
An r of -0.62 is a moderate relationship, well away from zero.

items.q: A student says the table proves that checking a phone often causes distraction. Which response is best?
options: The student is right, because 0.71 is a strong correlation
The correlation is negative, so phones reduce distraction
The student is right, because the survey had 400 students
Distracted students may check phones more: direction is unclear

why.correct: Even a strong correlation cannot show which variable affects the other, or rule out a third variable such as boredom or anxiety.
options: Strength does not turn a correlation into a cause.
The r is +0.71, positive.
A large sample does not show cause either.
Right: the directionality problem, plus possible third variables.
